cards.front: What are the three levels of a JavaFX application's structure?
cards.back: Stage (window) → Scene (root of the graph) → Node tree
cards.extra: A Stage holds one Scene; the Scene holds a tree of Nodes. Swapping the Scene changes the whole screen at once.

cards.back: The base class of every component in the scene graph
cards.extra: Controls, shapes, containers and canvas all extend it, so anything you add to the graph is a Node.

cards.back: A window in a desktop application
cards.extra: stage.setScene(...) then stage.show(). The primary stage arrives as a parameter to start(Stage).

cards.back: The base class for layout panes — components that arrange their children
cards.extra: Pane, HBox, VBox, GridPane extend it. Controls do too, which is why CSS padding and borders apply to both.

cards.back: HBox lays children out horizontally; VBox vertically
cards.extra: Both are single-axis: for wrapping rows, use FlowPane instead.

cards.back: Laying children in a row (or column) and wrapping to the next line when space runs out
cards.extra: The layout for tag clouds, galleries and anything responsive without a fixed grid.

cards.back: Placing children in a grid of rows and columns, with per-cell spanning
cards.extra: The most precise built-in layout, and the most verbose: you specify row/column indices for every node.

cards.back: Lays children out in a grid of equally sized tiles
cards.extra: Unlike GridPane the cells are uniform, which makes it the choice for icon boards and keypads.

cards.front: What is the difference between Group and Pane?
cards.back: Group applies no layout and sizes itself to its children; Pane is a resizable region that can be styled
cards.extra: Group for fixed-position graphics, Pane when you want a styled container that takes part in layout.

cards.front: What does JavaFX Canvas give you that the scene graph does not?
cards.back: Immediate-mode drawing through a GraphicsContext: paths, text, images, pixel-level control
cards.extra: Nodes are retained-mode objects; the canvas is a bitmap you repaint yourself. Use it for charts, games and custom visuals.

cards.back: With CSS, applied to nodes by type, id or style class
cards.extra: Same separation as HTML: .button { -fx-background-color: ...; }. JavaFX CSS is its own dialect with -fx- property names.

cards.back: An observable value that can be listened to and bound to other properties
cards.extra: Binding is what keeps the UI in sync with the model: change the model, the control updates itself.

cards.front: What is the fundamental threading rule in JavaFX?
cards.back: Only the JavaFX Application Thread may modify the scene graph
cards.extra: Do work on a background thread and hand results back with Platform.runLater. Touching nodes off-thread throws or corrupts the UI.

cards.front: How do you run work in the background in JavaFX?
cards.back: A Task or Service on an ExecutorService, updating the UI from its handlers
cards.extra: Task exposes updateProgress/updateMessage, which are safe to call from the worker thread.

cards.front: What is the difference between CheckBox and RadioButton?
cards.back: A checkbox toggles independently; radio buttons are grouped so only one is selected
cards.extra: JavaFX checkboxes also support an indeterminate third state, which is easy to forget when reading the state.

cards.front: What is the difference between ChoiceBox and ComboBox?
cards.back: ComboBox is editable and richer; ChoiceBox is a simple fixed list
cards.extra: ChoiceBox is lighter; ComboBox lets the user type a value or filter the list.

cards.back: From TableColumn cell value factories that read a property off the row object
cards.extra: The table knows nothing about your class: each column is told how to extract its field.

cards.back: A geometric operation — translate, rotate, scale, shear — applied on top of a node's layout
cards.extra: Node convenience methods such as setRotate and setScaleX are shorthand; the Transform classes allow composition.

cards.back: Visual post-processing on a node: drop shadow, blur, glow, reflection
cards.extra: They render in a separate pass, so they are not free — avoid them on large animated subtrees.

cards.front: How is animation done in JavaFX?
cards.back: Timeline with keyframes, or the transition classes such as FadeTransition and TranslateTransition
cards.extra: All of them drive properties over time, so animation and the property-binding system are the same machinery.

cards.back: Embeds a web engine so the app can render HTML and run JavaScript
cards.extra: Paired with WebEngine for navigation and script calls.

cards.back: Modal dialogs for picking a file or a directory
cards.extra: They live in javafx.stage, not the scene package, and can only be customised slightly.

cards.front: What is the JavaFX media package for?
cards.back: Playing audio and video through Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView
cards.extra: The player is the controller (play/pause/seek); the view is the node that displays frames.
